name: Explaining Research After Publication
title: Explaining Research After Publication
answer: Explaining research after publication covers the work of translating a peer-reviewed or preprint paper into forms that non-specialists, practitioners, journalists, and other researchers can use. It includes author-written blog posts, press releases, plain-language summaries, social media threads, commentaries, podcasts, and post-publication peer review. The aim is not to replace the paper but to clarify its question, method, findings, limits, and relation to prior work. In AI research, this often means explaining model evaluations, datasets, benchmarks, or claims about capability and risk without overstating what the study shows. The site's library of 135 research papers and 12,993 extracted claims is one example of a corpus where such explanations can be traced back to specific published statements.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Post-publication explanation runs on the published record and the platforms that carry it. The original paper, its supplementary material, code and data repositories, and any correction or retraction notices form the evidence base. Distribution happens through journals, preprint servers, institutional repositories, lab websites, newsletters, social media, and conference channels. Persistent identifiers such as DOIs and ORCID iDs help keep the link between an explanation and the work it describes. A site that links to the original paper rather than to the Consensus search tool keeps that chain of provenance visible.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with a close reading of the paper, its methods, results, and limitations. The explainer then restates the central claim in plain language, defines technical terms, and separates what the authors measured from what they infer. Authors may check drafts with co-authors, press offices, or communications staff, while independent explainers may seek comment from the authors or other experts. Good practice includes linking to the original paper, citing specific sections or figures, and noting any uncertainty, conflict of interest, or disagreement in the field. For AI topics, that often means explaining benchmarks, baselines, evaluation conditions, and the difference between a model's output and a scientific finding.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Post-publication explanation raises questions about copyright, licensing, and author rights, because papers and figures may be reused under different terms. Press embargoes, institutional review, and journal policies can shape what authors say and when they say it. Risks include oversimplification, hype, selective citation, loss of context, and the spread of claims that the paper does not support. Provenance matters: explanations typically point to the original paper, its version, and any corrections or retractions, and they distinguish the authors' claims from later commentary. This site's practice of linking to the original paper, not to the Consensus search tool, is one way to keep that provenance clear.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Explanations after publication are likely to become more structured and more traceable as publishers, repositories, and research tools adopt persistent identifiers and machine-readable metadata. AI-assisted summarization may speed up first drafts, but it also increases the risk of fluent errors, so human review and clear attribution remain central. Post-publication peer review, replication reports, and living reviews may grow as ways to update the record when new evidence appears. For AI research, the pressure to explain models, datasets, and evaluations to policy and industry audiences will keep growing. The field will need shared norms for what counts as a faithful explanation and how to correct one when it goes wrong.
